name: Kongo
confidence_why: Bentley 1887, Laman 1922 and Tavares 1915, three independent descriptions of different Kongo varieties, all place the main accent on the first syllable of the stem with prefixes not counting, and the only dissent, Visseq 1889's hedged antepenult-or-penult rule for the Kakongo (Cabinda) dialect, is a two-sentence note on a different dialect that admits placement must be learned from usage.
catalog_citation: Bentley, W. Holman. 1887. Dictionary and Grammar of the Kongo Language, as spoken at San Salvador, the Ancient Capital of the Old Kongo Empire, West Africa. London: Baptist Missionary Society / Trubner & Co.
catalog_locator: Grammar, section 'ACCENT', pp. 701-703 (archive.org item dictionarygramma00bent, djvu text)
catalog_quote: The accent in Kongo falls upon the first syllable of the stem. When more than two syllables follow the first syllable of the stem, a secondary and weaker accent falls upon the penult. It is upon the first syllable of the stem that the accent falls, not upon the first syllable of the word; prefixes, therefore, do not affect the question. If a verb possesses prefixes to the extent of two or more syllables, the first of such prefix-syllables receives also a slight accent. ... Dissyllabic words are accented on their last syllable according to the foregoing rule. ... In the case of maki, meso, dinu, maji, the first syllables are euphonic combinations of a prefix with an initial vowel, and are therefore accented. A few dissyllabic words take the accent on the first syllable although it is a prefix ... Sundry disturbing factors tend to interfere with the even application of the above rule. Th…
sweep_summary: The single works with stress in the title, Descourvières 1776 'Essay d'une grammaire congo, suivant l'accent Kakongo ou Malemba', is a false title hit: 'accent' = the Kakongo dialect. It is nonetheless a first-hand grammar of Kakongo, a Glottolog dialect of sans1272, and I located and read it in full — the Cuénot copy (24 fol., 49 images) is digitised at the Bibliothèque municipale de Besançon as Ms 523 (memoirevive.besancon.fr/ark:/48565/fhlcwkq0trmj; images. It is silent on word stress: fol. 1r gives an 18-letter alphabet and says only that inaudible vowels are marked with a breve and 'excessively long syllables' with a macron; later pages note elision of verb-final -a and an interrogative final open ê. Also read and silent: the Landana mission's 1890 Dictionnaire français-fiote (dialecte du Kakongo), Ussel 1888 Petite grammaire de la langue fiote (Loango dialect, Gallica; long/short marks only), Proyart 1776 ch. XIX, and Drieghe 2014 (UGent MA thesis on the 1772 Kakongo dictionary, open PDF; it fixes the manuscript's provenance and cites van Bulck 1959 Kongo-Overzee 20(2) and Nsondé 1995). No new stress statement for sans1272 was found; the catalog's Bentley-based coding is neither confirmed nor contradicted, and the prior check's identity problem (Bentley = Kisikongo/koon1244, not this coastal languoid) stands. Best remaining lead: Carrie 1890 'Grammaire de la langue fiote, dialecte du Kakongo' (Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description for sans1272) is full-view on Google Books (qTpAAAAAYAAJ) and HathiTrust (hvd.hx51gh) but both hosts refuse our network's egress (not reachable by automated download) — download it from another host; secondarily Mingas 1989 'Esquisse phonologique de l'Oyo' (Paris V DEA, print only). Doke 1959 (T&F, paywalled) describes the Rome copy only. searching used Glottolog, Gallica SRU, archive.org, Crossref, Europeana, UGent Primo, the local Glottolog 5.1 sources.bib and the local HathiTrust hathifile.

tone_statements.citation: Dom, Sebastian, Gilles-Maurice de Schryver & Koen Bostoen. 2020. Kisikongo (Bantu, H16a) present-future isomorphism: A diachronic conspiracy between semantics and phonology. Journal of Historical Linguistics 10(2): 251-288 (reprinted 2022 in Benjamins Current Topics 123, doi 10.1075/bct.123.04dom). Author postprint, UPSpace, University of Pretoria.
tone_statements.quote: Although Ndonga Mfuwa (1995) does note tone, he provides no examples of the simple present Ø-R-a. Out of the ten examples of the future Ø-R-a construction that are found in the grammatical description, there are nine instances where the vowel of the verb root is marked with a high tone. ... From this small dataset, one might infer that the tone pattern of the future construction is characterized by a high tone on the root vowel which undergoes rightward spread to the next syllable or any other syllable that is not word-final. ... The currently available data is too limited for a detailed tone analysis. However, the simple present and future constructions seem to have identical tone patterns.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 3.4 'Overview and discussion', postprint pp. 23-24 (exx. 36-38); fn. 13 p. 18 on Bentley writing no tone
tone_statements.summary: Kisikongo has lexical/grammatical H tone written by Ndonga Mfuwa 1995; in the future (and residual simple present) O-R-a verb form a H sits on the first root syllable and spreads rightward onto following non-final syllables (CV́CV, CV́:NCV, CV́CV́CV); word-final syllable stays L; one variant with H on the subject prefix; no inventory, TBU or downstep analysis given; nothing on stress.

audit.recode_to: Move the Bentley-1887-based coding to koon1244 (Kisikongo = kisi1245 under South-Central Koongo) and merge it with the existing koon1244 'Koongo' record, resolving that record's conflicting 'fixed-strict stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable) (word-initial) coding in favour of 'morphological' (stem-initial main accent, prefixes excluded, secondary penult) — Bentley p. 701 says explicitly 'not upon the first syllable of the word', and Laman 1922 §2 and Tavares 1915 §2 independently agree. The sans1272 slot (Glottolog's West-Kikongo coastal languoid) then has no valid source; re-source it from Mingas 1994 / Visseq 1889 or leave it empty.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim in the Bentley djvu text we hold at the stated place (pp. 701-703). (2) Source: an 1887 missionary dictionary-grammar, pre-tonological; the modern grammar of the same variety (Ndonga Mfuwa 1995) marks tone and is not yet obtained or open. (3) Identity: Glottolog tags Bentley 1887 to koon1244, and Glottolog 5.1's sans1272, despite the legacy name 'San Salvador Kongo' [kwy], is a West-Kikongo coastal languoid (dialects Iwoyo, Kakongo, Ciwoyo, Cisundi Cabinda…; Glottolog's most extensive descriptions Mingas 1994 Iwoyo, Carrie 1890 Kakongo) for which Bentley is not a description. (4) Duplicate: the catalog already has a koon1244 'Koongo' record resting on the very same Bentley passage (via the StressTyp2 entry for this language) but coded fixed-strict word-initial, contradicting this record's 'morphological' coding; Bentley's own wording ('not upon the first syllable of the word; prefixes … do not affect the question'), Laman

sources.citation: Laman, K. E. 1922. The Musical Accent or Intonation in the Kongo Language. Stockholm: Svenska Missionsförbundets Förlag. (archive.org musicalaccentori00lamarich)
sources.quote: 'The dynamic accent can be divided ... into the root-accent and the rhythmic accent ... a) The root-accent always falls on the root-syllable. ... Prefixes, as a rule, have no influence on the accent: kiese, joy; kibulu, animal; wabatonda, he loved them. ... b) The rhythmic accent is a secondary accent that always falls on the penult.' §28: 'The strong stress in the Kongo language may be placed on different syllables ... because pitch and position in the sentence may have a strong influence upon the accent.' (Central Kongo/Mukimbungu variety, same Glottolog language koon1244 as Bentley's Kisiko
sources.note: Only dedicated prosody monograph for the Kongo cluster (Central Kongo, same Glottolog language koon1244 as Bentley's variety); separates dynamic accent from pitch and states root-syllable accent with prefixes excluded and rhythmic penult secondary, independently confirming the morphological reading of Bentley.

sources.citation: Tavares, José Lourenço. 1915. Gramática da língua do Congo (kikongo), dialecto kisolongo. Luanda. (archive.org gramticadalnguad00tava)
sources.quote: General rule for primitive words: 'As de duas sílabas tem acento predominante, regra geral, na primeira delas. As de mais de duas sílabas tem acento predominante ... na penúltima.' But: 'Se a palavra é composta, derivada, ou sofreu alteração por motivo de flexão, então, qualquer que seja o número de sílabas ... conserva, regra geral, o acento predominante na mesma sílaba em que o teria como palavra primitiva (lungisa < lunga, balama < bala) ... As palavras primitivas ... em que entre qualquer dos prefixos, tem acento predominante na sílaba radical: isto é, na sílaba que se segue a êsse prefixo
sources.locator: '3.º Da acentuação' p. 4 (djvu lines 750-760) and '§ 2.º Da acentuação' c. pp. 72-73 (lines 6637-6675)
sources.note: Kisolongo (South Kikongo, closest described sister of Kisikongo): accent on the radical syllable after the prefix, retained under derivation/inflection; second independent early witness for stem-syllable accent.

sources.citation: Visseq, Alexandre. 1889. Grammaire fiote, ou grammaire de la langue du Congo. Paris: Maisonneuve. (archive.org grammairefioteou00viss_0; Fiote of the Landana/Cabinda Holy Ghost mission = Kakongo, a dialect Glottolog lists under sans1272)
sources.quote: 'L'accent joue le plus grand rôle dans cette langue, au point que, si on ne l'observe pas, on n'est pas compris. Où se place-t-il? L'usage seul peut l'apprendre. Toutefois on peut donner, comme règles générales que, pour les mots de trois syllabes et plus, l'accent se trouve sur l'antépénultième, et sur la pénultième pour les mots de deux syllabes.' This describes the coastal languoid that Glottolog actually calls sans1272, and it is a length-based (antepenult/penult), hedged rule, not Bentley's stem-initial rule: if the record stays keyed to sans1272 its source base and coding would change.
sources.note: Open description of the Kakongo/Fiote coastal variety that Glottolog files under sans1272; its accent rule (antepenult in 3+-syllable words, penult in disyllables, 'l'usage seul peut l'apprendre') differs from Bentley's and shows the sans1272 slot is currently sourced from the wrong languoid.

sources.quote: No stress content; establishes identity: Kisikongo [kisi1245] is a dialect of South-Central Koongo [koon1244] (…> Southern Kikongo > Koongo-Kituba > South-Central Koongo > Southern Koongo), whereas held places sans1272 under West Kikongo [west2874] with Cabinda-coast dialects; Glottolog ref 39095 (Bentley 1887) is tagged to koon1244.

sources.note: Sec. 3.4 gives the only printed remarks on present-day Kisikongo verb tone: Bentley 1887 neither discusses nor writes tone (fn. 13); Ndonga Mfuwa 1995 marks tone; in his future O-R-a examples the root vowel carries H with rightward spread to following non-final syllables (okóta, otú:nga, osónéka), one example has H on the subject prefix instead; simple present yeela has the same pattern (beyééla 'they are/will be sick'); authors state the data are too limited for a detailed tone analysis. Not a tone study; historical TA morphology with a tone excursus.
